headline: Robot evaluation is moving past one success score toward human-perceived safety, failure boundaries, and the per-hardware cost of running the policy.
thesis: Several papers today refuse to let one aggregate number stand in for a robot's behaviour. A street-perception study finds that multimodal models and 25 human respondents both shift their safety choices at night, but the models pick the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often than people do. A haptic teleoperation study shows operators drive an underwater ROV faster with cross-current cues while reporting more mental demand and frustration. Failure-boundary profiles show that driving and navigation agents with similar scores stop or push through blocked passages in different ways, and a rollout-free checkpoint ranking tracks real-robot success better than validation loss. On the data and systems side, human-video pretraining follows a log-linear trend that only pays off when the data matches the robot, and VLA inference bottlenecks change from one GPU to the next.

clusters.title: Human-facing robot studies now measure perceived safety and workload, and these can move opposite to speed or task success
clusters.why: The usual robot paper reports success and time, but the papers here show operators and bystanders react on other axes. Haptic cues about unseen cross-currents made an ROV operator faster and more confident while raising mental demand and frustration. Persona-conditioned models chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often than the human respondents did, so model judgments cannot replace a human panel. A team building interactive robots should log workload, confidence and perceived safety next to task metrics, and should test the stimuli on people before relying on a model proxy.

clusters.title: Robot evaluations are moving from one success score to failure-boundary and mismatch diagnostics that expose hidden errors
clusters.why: Aggregate success hides which decision a robot made, such as stopping at a blocked corridor versus pushing through with contact. Failure-boundary profiles score commitment and competence along a measured factor, and the self-repair study finds that resampling and mismatched feedback must be baselines before credit goes to failure-specific feedback. Offline residual tests can flag swapped axes or inverted gripper polarity in held-out transitions before a policy runs. The practical change is to add stop-versus-proceed variants and matched baselines to any test suite used for release decisions.

clusters.title: Human data helps robot policies when its kinematic, visual and contact properties match the robot, not simply when it is larger
clusters.why: A large egocentric video corpus shows a log-linear relation between pretraining hours and robot success in simulation, which supports scaling human data. The survey in this set argues that recording volume matters less than alignment, and that shared action representations do not remove embodiment limits on force, latency and contact. Tactile results point the same way: separating marker flow, normal and depth cues changed success, with marker flow the strongest single cue. Before collecting more human video, a team should check which physical cue the task depends on and whether the human hand matches the robot hand.

clusters.title: VLA deployment cost is set by per-GPU bottlenecks, and compression or visual token routing cut it with small accuracy loss
clusters.why: The inference study notes that most published VLA speedups use a single GPU type, and finds that the limiting factor changes across datacenter and embedded hardware. Weight compression to INT2 reports a large storage reduction while staying close to the BF16 teacher on four embodied tasks, and visual token routing matches full-resolution performance with 2.5 to 5.8 times fewer tokens. A deployment team should profile its own target board first and then stack optimizations in the order the guidelines suggest, rather than adopting a single reported speedup.

clusters.title: Self-improvement loops on physical robots keep gains by storing skills or checking retention, not by retraining freely
clusters.why: Physical self-improvement can compound across stages, but the compounding method in this set adds a retention step that compares the inherited policy with the refined one before promotion. A real-world coding-agent framework keeps interaction experience and reusable executable skills as persistent memory, and reports success on eight real tasks. Multi-task online RL results show that the task distribution and value-based RL drive generalization to tasks not seen in training. For a team that updates policies on hardware, the lesson is to keep a promotion gate and a skill store rather than overwriting shared weights.

insights: Report human-facing measures next to task success. The persona study shows that multimodal models pick the delivery robot over the humanoid far more often than 25 human respondents do, and that a night effect for the humanoid is about three times larger in one model than in humans. The haptic ROV study shows the same split from the operator side: cues raised mental demand and frustration while operators drove faster. For a team of robots that share streets or workspaces, the next study should log perceived safety and workload from people on the same stimuli, and use models only as a cheap first screen, since the abstract says they capture only part of human judgment.

Evaluate where a robot should stop, not only how often it succeeds. The failure-boundary paper finds that a driving agent that pushes through blocked corridors averages 52.2 on blocked widths, while agents that stop average 37.8 to 40.6, so a driving score rewards the wrong choice. The same method, applied to a warehouse navigation policy in Isaac Sim, shows it stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families. Add stop-versus-proceed variants to your navigation tests, and when you evaluate self-repair agents, include resampling and mismatched-feedback baselines: the self-repair study finds fixed task guidance recovers about as well as feedback from other episodes, with no detected benefit from matching the failure label.

Buy human data for embodiment match, then for volume. The egocentric pretraining study reports a log-linear relation between hours and robot success, but its strongest robot numbers are in simulation, and the survey argues that the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment. The tactile study gives a concrete test: with 720 real-robot trials, its best single cue (marker flow) reached 74.4%, while the policy without tactile perception reached 57.8% and the full tactile setup 78.9%. Before adding a larger dataset, run a short ablation on the physical cue your task depends on, and check whether the human hand kinematics are close enough to the robot hand to transfer.

Profile VLA inference on the board you ship. The inference study covers seven VLAs and four GPU families from datacenter H100 to Jetson Thor, and it finds that CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth and kernel efficiency decide which optimization pays off. Weight compression to INT2 cut storage from 8.9 GB to 2.1 GB in one reported setting, and token routing reduced inference cost by up to 3.3 times, but the paper stresses that combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode. Measure your own latency budget on the target device first, then apply the stacking guidance in that order.

must_read.why: It is the clearest direct comparison in this batch of how robot presence changes perceived safety, and it measures models against human respondents on the same question.
must_read.key_idea: Perceived street safety is measured as a pairwise choice between otherwise matched images, which lets the paper compare no-robot, delivery-robot and humanoid conditions across time of day and road class.
must_read.evidence: 18 generated Seoul street images, 500 synthetic personas per model, 25 human respondents. Both models prefer streets without robots and favour the delivery robot over the humanoid; robots are chosen more often at night and by fewer older personas.
must_read.caveat: The images are generated rather than photographed, and the abstract reports no effect sizes or significance tests. It also covers pairwise choices only, not how people would behave around a robot.

must_read.why: It is one of the few field-style studies of operator cognition during robot teleoperation in this set, and it reports a trade-off a deployment team has to design for.
must_read.key_idea: Haptic cues about unseen cross-currents trade mental workload for confidence: operators reported higher mental demand and frustration with the cues, but drove the ROV faster.
must_read.evidence: An in-water ROV study with controlled cross-currents and a soft vibrating haptic touchpad. Unseen current raised physical and temporal demand; haptic cues reduced those and improved self-assessed performance.
must_read.caveat: The abstract gives no participant count and no statistics, and covers a single ROV setup in one in-water study, so the speed result should be read as a single-study signal.

must_read.why: It turns operator takeover into a training signal for the policy, with measured gains on real manipulation tasks, which is directly usable in a teleoperation-driven data loop.
must_read.key_idea: The operator previews the policy's predicted motion in XR and intervenes before an anticipated bad action; the rejected prediction and the corrective chunk from the same physical state form a preference pair for post-training.
must_read.evidence: Four real-world manipulation tasks. With five correction episodes per condition, success rose from 44.0% to 70.3% for a diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA, compared with HG-DAgger.
must_read.caveat: Five correction episodes per condition is a small correction budget, and the abstract does not say how many operators took part or how the XR interface affected their workload.

must_read.why: It changes how a navigation or driving stack should be judged when the right answer is sometimes to wait, and it includes a warehouse robot case, not only driving.
must_read.key_idea: Each scenario family varies one measured factor, each variant is labelled proceed or stop from measurement, and the commitment and competence curves show where an agent crosses one half.
must_read.evidence: Seven driving agents on seven CARLA families; the rule-based expert reaches decision accuracy 0.74 and the best learned agent, TFv6, 0.60. Applied to an Isaac Sim warehouse navigation policy, it stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families.
must_read.caveat: Most of the evidence is in CARLA driving, the warehouse part covers one policy and three families, and the proceed or stop labels depend on the paper's measurement rule.

2611.05954.problem: It is unclear how the presence and type of urban robots change the perceived safety of a street, and whether models can stand in for people when judging it.
2611.05954.method: Pairwise safety judgments on 18 generated Seoul street images varying time of day, road class and robot condition, made by two multimodal models conditioned on 500 synthetic personas each and by 25 human respondents.
2611.05954.why: A robotics team deploying delivery robots or humanoids in public should expect that models and people disagree on robot type, so a model panel is not enough to predict public reception.

2611.06689.problem: Operators of an ROV in hazardous water cannot see unseen cross-currents, which raises physical and mental workload and risks expensive hardware.
2611.06689.method: An in-water study in which a soft vibrating haptic touchpad presents environmental information to the operator under controlled cross-currents, compared with a current-only condition.
2611.06689.why: A teleoperation interface for any hazardous robot should be assessed on operator workload and confidence as well as on speed and task outcome, since these can point in different directions.

2611.05667.problem: Imitation policies fail in ways operators only notice after the fact, and standard interventions give the policy little usable signal for the failure.
2611.05667.method: PHIL shows the operator the policy's predicted trajectory in XR, lets them take over before an undesirable action, and post-trains the policy to prefer the corrective chunk over the rejected prediction from the same state.
2611.05667.why: It gives a teleoperation team a concrete way to turn takeovers into training data, with measured gains on both a diffusion policy and a pretrained VLA.

2611.06453.problem: Driving-style scores multiply route completion by an infraction penalty, so an agent that pushes through a blocked passage can score the same as one that waits.
2611.06453.method: Failure-boundary profiles vary one measured factor per scenario family, certify each variant as proceed or stop, and estimate commitment and competence curves with run-to-run intervals.
2611.06453.why: A navigation team can use the same stop-versus-proceed test on a warehouse robot, where the abstract reports the tested policy stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families.

2611.06068.problem: Swarm robots are hard to direct for tasks that need different behaviour, such as flowing around obstacles in one moment and pushing objects the next.
2611.06068.method: Fluidic Body places a virtual fluid between the user's hand and the swarm, so hand opening and closing change the swarm between soft and cohesive modes.
2611.06068.why: It is an example of an interaction metaphor that a human-robot interface team could borrow, with a VR study of 17 participants and a physical demonstration with 88 participants.

2611.06863.problem: Code-as-policy agents retry failed programs, but it is unclear whether the gain comes from failure-specific feedback or from simply sampling more programs.
2611.06863.method: On 252 initial failures in simulated manipulation, a frozen code model regenerates programs under different feedback templates, mismatched feedback, task guidance, and plain resampling.
2611.06863.why: A team building self-repairing robot code should include resampling and mismatched-feedback baselines, because the abstract finds resampling alone recovers 68.3% against 85.3% for the feedback variant.

2611.06653.problem: A robot action can satisfy shape and range checks yet carry the wrong semantics, such as swapped axes or reversed gripper polarity, and such mismatches go unnoticed.
2611.06653.method: Learned state-action-effect models are calibrated on clean held-out transitions to raise alarms at a fixed false-positive rate, and a closed-set inverse vocabulary ranks the likely mismatched field.
2611.06653.why: An offline check like this could run on logged data before a new action interface is deployed, but the abstract frames it as a bounded diagnostic rather than a deployment safety guarantee.

2611.05838.problem: Validation loss is a poor predictor of which policy checkpoint will succeed on the robot, and real-robot trials per checkpoint are expensive.
2611.05838.method: RACE scores checkpoints on a fixed set of held-out successful trajectories by calibrating action deviations against state-conditional thresholds and aggregating them with a running product.
2611.05838.why: A team choosing checkpoints without many trials can use it as a rollout-free filter, since the abstract reports rankings that align with deployment success on real robots.

2611.06817.problem: Robot policies trained on little robot data do not benefit clearly from human video, and the scaling behaviour of human data is unclear.
2611.06817.method: Open-HumanScale curates a 50,000-hour egocentric corpus annotated with hand motion and language, measures a log-linear scaling law against simulated robot success, and trains a world-action model on it with and without robot data.
2611.06817.why: It gives a data strategy for a team collecting human video, with the caveat that the strongest robot numbers in the abstract come from simulated benchmarks.

2611.06724.problem: Dexterous hardware, data, cross-embodiment transfer and evaluation are usually reviewed separately, so claims about foundation models for hands are hard to compare.
2611.06724.method: A structured narrative survey organized in five layers, with comparative tables and five case analyses, that separates within-study comparisons from corpus statistics and vendor claims.
2611.06724.why: A team building or buying dexterous hands gets eleven open problems and a warning that task completion alone does not establish deployment readiness.

2611.06673.problem: Visuo-tactile policies take raw tactile images as input, so it is unclear which physical cues contribute to learning.
2611.06673.method: Tactile RGB, normal or depth maps and marker-flow fields are derived from the same stream and compared with the same policy backbone over 720 real-robot trials, including fusion strategies.
2611.06673.why: It shows that marker flow alone reached 74.4% success against 57.8% without tactile input, so a team should pick a tactile representation for the stage of contact their task needs.

2611.06710.problem: VLA inference can exceed a robot's real-time budget, and published optimizations are usually measured on one GPU and a few models.
2611.06710.method: A measurement study of seven optimization families on seven VLAs across four GPU families, analysing launch overhead, memory bandwidth and kernel efficiency, and deriving VLA-Triage guidelines for stacking them.
2611.06710.why: A deployment team on embedded hardware such as Jetson-class boards should measure its own bottleneck before choosing among quantization, pruning and graph capture.

2611.06075.problem: Deploying a separate adapter per skill on an edge robot multiplies memory and management cost for a vision-language model.
2611.06075.method: UniCompress distills a BF16 Qwen3-VL-4B teacher into an asymmetric INT2 student with GPTQ initialization and teacher-guided quantization recovery across the vision encoder and language backbone.
2611.06075.why: It reports weight storage falling from 8.9 GB to 2.1 GB and a macro score within 0.9 points of the BF16 teacher on four embodied tasks, which is the relevant trade-off for a single on-robot model.

2611.06854.problem: Computer-use and real-time agents spend most of their compute on visual tokens that are either irrelevant to the next action or repeated across screenshots.
2611.06854.method: Visual Token Routing trains a lightweight spatio-temporal router jointly with the vision-language model so that only selected image-region tokens enter the language model.
2611.06854.why: The abstract reports matching full-resolution performance on OSWorld, CUA-World and video game action prediction with 2.5 to 5.8 times fewer tokens, which is a template for trimming perception cost on a robot's camera stream.

2611.06654.problem: Generalist robot policies trained offline stall because failures in later stages stay hidden until earlier stages pass, and updates can erase skills already learned.
2611.06654.method: Compounding Physical RSI runs three stages: stage-level capability-gap assessment, offline behaviour-regularized RL on curated experience, and a retention stage that promotes the best weight-space candidate between the reference and refined policies.
2611.06654.why: On the RoboDojo-Sim leaderboard the paper reports a three-seed mean Overall Score of 26.15 across 42 tasks, and its retention gate is a concrete pattern for any team updating shared policy weights.

2611.06768.problem: Coding agents that write robot programs need a way to turn physical exploration into lasting, reusable skills rather than one-off fixes.
2611.06768.method: PyRUA-REAL keeps interaction experience and executable skills as persistent memory that informs later exploration and code refinement, and deploys the resulting programs without an online agent.
2611.06768.why: It reports 91.1% average success over eight real-world tasks and 84.4% on 42 RoboDojo tasks, which suggests a skill store is a practical component for a robot that must keep improving after deployment.

2611.06905.problem: Online RL improvement has mostly targeted one narrow deployment task, while the base robot policy is multi-task.
2611.06905.method: A structured evaluation of value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation choices for improving a generalist policy online across many tasks at once.
2611.06905.why: The abstract reports that generalization to tasks not seen in online training depends on the training task distribution and on value-based RL, which bears on how a team should choose its improvement tasks.

2611.06908.problem: Humanoid autonomy is limited by the lack of paired vision, language and joint-command data at scale, and teleoperation data costs human time.
2611.06908.method: HALO synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes and trains skills such as sitting, navigating to named objects, crouching and pushing boxes, which it orchestrates into long-horizon tasks.
2611.06908.why: It reports 91% success over 360 real-world trials in six unmapped environments, which is one of the more direct real-world signals in this batch for a humanoid team.

2611.05658.problem: Brain-to-robot decoders are judged by single-trial accuracy, which may not predict planning regret in sequential assistive control.
2611.05658.method: The paper models brain-to-robot control as a POMDP and derives a closed-form regret predictor computed from a decoder's confusion matrix.
2611.05658.why: It shows two decoders with the same 35.1% validation accuracy on real EEG data differ 9.6 times in held-out regret, which argues for evaluating assistive decoders on planning outcomes.

2611.06442.problem: Online real-world RL in a laboratory needs many costly demonstrations and dense rewards that are hard to get from the physical scene.
2611.06442.method: A digital twin built from 3D Gaussian splatting and physics simulation supplies policy pretraining and a visual reward model, which provides dense rewards during human-in-the-loop refinement.
2611.06442.why: The abstract reports 98% mean autonomous success across five real laboratory tasks with at most 25 minutes of real interaction per task, which is a practical budget for a lab-automation team.

2611.06702.problem: Ground robots in off-road terrain need help from aerial sensing, but continuous aerial mapping costs too much flight time.
2611.06702.method: The UGV scores its own MPPI rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, requests an aerial measurement only when resolving uncertainty improves predicted navigation, and replans after fusing the result.
2611.06702.why: It reports 98.9% goal attainment in 180 simulated trials with 87.7% less UAV flight time than continuous greedy mapping, and field runs over about 2 km, which is a usable pattern for heterogeneous teams.

2611.06913.problem: Torque-limited, payload-aware collision-free motion planning has to be fast enough for repeated pick-and-place cycles on a real arm.
2611.06913.method: B-spline trajectory optimization with a GPU time-optimal stage that solves banded Newton systems under velocity, acceleration, jerk and torque constraints.
2611.06913.why: The abstract reports 4.4 ms mean planning time on an RTX 5090 with a 3 kg payload, 14.7 times faster than cuRoboV2, and a stereo deployment on the YAM arm, which matters for cycle time on a real cell.

2611.06196.problem: MPC and RL safety guarantees usually rely on control-invariant sets, which are hard to compute for nonlinear robots.
2611.06196.method: New classes of safe sets constrain nodes of the prediction horizon rather than only the terminal state, and an inner approximation supports a safe-abort strategy when recursive feasibility fails.
2611.06196.why: The paper reports fewer constraint violations than the compared methods on a 6-joint manipulator in simulation, with hardware experiments, and gives a route to safety guarantees for learned controllers.
